claims.claim: DeepMind published SynthID Bio in Nature on 2026-09-30, a family of methods for watermarking AI-generated protein sequences and predicted structures to establish provenance.

The sequence watermark applies SynthID-Text's tournament-based token-selection to ProteinMPNN's per-residue logits, biasing amino-acid choice during decoding rather than editing the sequence afterward.

Detection computes a mean g-value per sequence: an unwatermarked baseline sits near 0.50 (~0.5037), a non-distortionary setting rises to ~0.589, and a stronger distortionary setting reaches ~0.890 in the released example tests.

Watermarked binders were wet-lab tested against three targets (VEGF-A, SARS-CoV-2 spike RBD, PD-L1) and matched unwatermarked designs on hit rate, binding affinity and sequence diversity, but the parity is stated qualitatively with no numbers in public material.
DeepMind explicitly frames SynthID Bio as a proof of concept and lists resistance to deliberate tampering as an unsolved challenge.

The structure watermark is baked into AlphaFold 3 weights so predicted coordinates carry a detectable signature regardless of who runs the model, with DeepMind claiming near-perfect detectability robust to digital noise and minor coordinate changes.

A protein-sequence watermark must hide its signal in functionally neutral positions to avoid impairing function, but those same neutral positions are exactly what an adversary can freely mutate to strip it.
SynthID-Text, the text analogue, is a statistical watermark whose detection strengthens with length and degrades under paraphrase, confirming that short, low-entropy channels carry weaker signal.

A watermark proves AI-origin, which is orthogonal to hazard; DNA-synthesis screening today matches ordered sequences by homology against lists of sequences of concern, detecting resemblance to known hazards, not provenance.

Executive Order 14110 (2023-10-30) makes procurement from screening-compliant providers a condition of federal research funding rather than a universal mandate, so it does not reach actors who take no federal funds.
List-based screening is acknowledged in US policy analysis to be incomplete and evadable by capable actors through minor sequence modification.

As a screening signal the watermark functions as a whitelist, not a detector: an absent watermark is uninformative because a natural sequence, an unwatermarked model's output, and a stripped sequence look identical to a screener.

The watermark only binds outputs of models that embed it; open-weight protein design tools and adversaries simply produce unmarked sequences, so a detection mandate fails while a provenance (fast-track) mandate can still work.

The operationally credible near-term use is positive provenance: letting synthesis providers fast-track orders proven to come from a trusted, safeguarded model, as described by a Twist Bioscience reviewer.
No DNA-synthesis provider had announced adoption or integration at publication; SynthID Bio is open-sourced research code and weights, not a commercial or deployed screening product.
The canonical dual-use precedent, Urbina et al. (2022), inverted a drug-discovery model's toxicity objective to generate roughly 40,000 candidate harmful molecules in under six hours.

A 2024 RAND red-team of 45 participants found no statistically significant difference in the viability of attack plans produced with versus without current large language models, tempering the urgency premise behind watermark mandates.

The lowest-friction near-term application is database integrity: keeping self-identifying AI proteins out of or labeled within PDB, UniProt and GenBank, where mislabeling is usually accidental so robustness to deliberate tampering is not the bar.
The method was extended beyond proteins to a bacteriophage genome designed with the Evo 2 model, reported to remain functional in early bacterial-culture tests, but weakly sourced and unquantified.

A detectability figure in the paper covers only binders that pass a g-value threshold at a 0.1% false-positive rate, implying a selection effect where the true-positive rate is not guaranteed to be 100% across all designs.
